q: Which of these is an accessory digestive organ rather than a part of the alimentary canal?
options: Pancreas
Esophagus
Pharynx
Large intestine

q: Select every example of mechanical digestion.
options: Your molars grinding a peanut
An enzyme in saliva splitting starch into sugars
The stomach wall churning its contents
Rings of intestinal muscle chopping and remixing the contents
Glucose crossing the intestinal lining into the blood
Protein being split into amino acids
misconception: mechanical and chemical digestion are the same process

q: Put the parts of the small intestine's wall in order, from the lumen outward.
options: Simple columnar epithelium
Lamina propria
Submucosa
Circular layer of smooth muscle
Longitudinal layer of smooth muscle
Serosa (visceral peritoneum)

q: Name the pinned layer of the GI wall.
options: Submucosa
Mucosa
Muscularis
Serosa

fig.alt: A cutaway drawing of a short length of digestive tube with its layers peeled back like nested sleeves. From the central space outward: an inner lining with glands and small patches of lymphoid tissue, a thin muscle layer, a connective tissue layer carrying blood vessels, nerves and a nerve network, a ring of circular muscle and a sheet of lengthwise muscle with a second nerve network between them, and a thin outer covering. A sheet of tissue carrying an artery, a vein and a nerve attaches the tube to the body wall.

q: Name the pinned nerve network.
options: Myenteric plexus
Submucosal plexus
Vagus nerve
Celiac ganglion

fig.alt: A cutaway drawing of a short length of digestive tube with its layers peeled back like nested sleeves. From the central space outward: an inner lining with glands and small patches of lymphoid tissue, a thin muscle layer, a connective tissue layer carrying blood vessels, nerves and a nerve network, a ring of circular muscle and a sheet of lengthwise muscle with a second nerve network between them, and a thin outer covering. A sheet of tissue carrying an artery, a vein and a nerve attaches the tube to the body wall.

q: This pathway describes one peristaltic wave. Which step is wrong?
options: Food stretches a short length of the wall
Enteric sensory neurons detect the stretch
Circular muscle behind the food contracts
Circular muscle ahead of the food also contracts, gripping it
The food is pushed forward and stretches the next length of wall
misconception: peristalsis is just a squeeze behind the food

q: In an experiment, a length of intestine shows strong rings of contraction that form, relax and re-form between the old rings, but no wave travels along it. What is its contents most likely doing?
options: Moving quickly along the tube toward the anus
Being pushed back up toward the stomach
Being absorbed while the contents stay unmixed
Being mixed while staying in about the same place

q: A newborn has not passed stool, and his abdomen is swelling. A biopsy shows that the last stretch of his large intestine has no enteric neurons in its wall; the intestine above it is normal. The segment without neurons is narrow and tightly contracted. Why does this segment block the passage of stool?
options: Its muscle has no nerve input, so it is paralyzed and floppy
Its mucosa cannot absorb water, so stool becomes too large to pass
Its sympathetic fibers are missing, so its sphincters stay open
Its circular muscle cannot relax, so no peristaltic wave can pass

q: A student sprinting to catch a train has strong sympathetic activity. Predict the change in each variable in her stomach and intestines, compared with resting after a meal.

variables.name: Secretion by glands in the gut wall

q: A fatty, acidic mixture from the stomach enters the first part of the small intestine. Predict the change in each variable over the next few minutes.
Stretch of the stomach wall sends signals up the vagus nerve to the brainstem, which sends signals back down the vagus that increase acid secretion. What kind of reflex is this?
options: A long reflex
A short reflex
A somatic reflex
A hormonal reflex

q: Fill the gap: Acid from the stomach enters the first part of the small intestine → ______ → the pancreas and the ducts that carry bile release bicarbonate-rich fluid → the acid is neutralized → the stimulus is removed
options: Gastrin is released into the blood
Motilin is released into the blood
Secretin is released into the blood
The myenteric plexus stops all contractions

q: Which organ is retroperitoneal?
options: Stomach
Most of the small intestine
Gallbladder
Pancreas

q: During surgery for a burst appendix, the surgeon finds a fatty sheet of tissue stuck to the inflamed area, walling it off from the rest of the abdomen. It hangs from the stomach in front of the intestines. What is it?
options: The lesser omentum
The parietal peritoneum
The greater omentum
The mesentery of the small intestine

q: In a laboratory, a length of guinea pig intestine is placed in warm, oxygenated salt solution with no nerves connecting it to the brain or spinal cord. A small pellet is put in one end. What happens to the pellet?
options: It stays put until vagal signals are supplied to the muscle
Peristalsis run by the wall's own neurons pushes it along
It moves only after epinephrine is added to the solution
It is squeezed by the whole length contracting at once

q: An antibiotic that happens to stimulate motilin's receptor proteins is sometimes given to a patient whose stomach empties too slowly. What does the drug imitate?
options: The hormone that makes the gallbladder contract after a fatty meal
The hormone that raises acid secretion by the stomach
The hormone that triggers clearing contractions between meals
The hormone that releases bicarbonate from the pancreas

q: Name the pinned layer of membrane.
options: Parietal peritoneum
Visceral peritoneum
Peritoneal cavity
Greater omentum

fig.alt: A cross section through the upper abdomen, with the back at the top of the drawing. A thick blue-green band traces a membrane that lines the inside of the body wall and folds inward to wrap the stomach, the intestines, the liver and the spleen, leaving a thin space between its two layers. The kidneys and pancreas sit against the back wall, behind the membrane.

q: Pacesetter cells in the stomach produce slow waves about 3 times a minute. After a meal, the stomach contracts about 3 times a minute; during the quiet stretches between meals it barely contracts, though the slow waves continue. What explains the difference?
options: Between meals the pacesetter cells slow to less than once a minute
Nerve and hormone signals after a meal push each slow wave past threshold
After a meal the stomach switches from smooth to skeletal muscle control
Between meals the gap junctions between the muscle cells close completely

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Uvula
Soft palate
Palatine tonsil
Lingual frenulum

fig.alt: A front view into a wide-open mouth. The upper and lower rows of teeth form two arches, with flat cutting teeth at the front, a pointed tooth at each corner and broad grinding teeth toward the back. Above is the bony front of the roof of the mouth and the soft back part with a small hanging flap in the middle. Arches of tissue at the back frame the opening to the throat, with a tonsil between them on each side. The tongue is raised, showing the fold of tissue under it and small duct openings on the floor of the mouth. Folds join the lips to the gums at the midline.

q: Name the pinned tissue of the tooth.
options: Enamel
Dentin
Cementum
Pulp

fig.alt: A lengthwise cut through a molar sitting in its socket of bone. The part above the gum is capped with a hard outer layer. Beneath it, a thick layer makes up most of the tooth and surrounds a central cavity that holds blood vessels and a nerve; the cavity continues down each root as a narrow canal. A thin layer covers the roots, and fibers attach it to the bone of the socket. Brackets mark the crown, the neck at the gum line and the roots.

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Upper esophageal sphincter
Lower esophageal sphincter
Diaphragm
Trachea

fig.alt: A side view of the head, neck and chest cut down the middle. A narrow muscular tube runs from the throat, behind the windpipe, down through the chest to the stomach. Labels mark a sphincter at its upper end, just below the throat, and another at its lower end, where it joins the stomach.

q: A 5-year-old has a complete set of deciduous teeth. Which kind of tooth is missing from that set but present in the adult set?
options: Incisors
Canines (cuspids)
Premolars
Molars

q: A dentist drills a small cavity. The patient feels nothing while the drill is in the enamel and flinches as it goes deeper. Which tissue has the drill just reached?
options: Cementum
The periodontal ligament
Pulp
Dentin

q: After a stroke in the medulla oblongata, a patient can chew and push food to the back of his mouth, but thin liquids trickle into his larynx and make him cough. Which part of swallowing is failing?
options: The voluntary phase, started by the cerebral cortex and the tongue
The pharyngeal phase, run by the brainstem swallowing center
The esophageal phase, carried out by peristalsis in the esophagus
Secretion of saliva by the glands that lubricate the bolus

q: Put these events of a swallow in order.
options: The tongue presses the bolus against the hard palate and back into the oropharynx
Sensory signals from the oropharynx reach the swallowing center in the brainstem
The soft palate seals the nasopharynx and the vocal folds close
The larynx rises, the epiglottis tips down, and the upper esophageal sphincter opens
A peristaltic wave carries the bolus down the esophagus
The bolus passes the relaxed lower esophageal sphincter into the stomach

q: This sequence describes the pharyngeal phase of a swallow. Which step is wrong?
options: The soft palate and uvula lift and seal the nasopharynx
The vocal folds close
The larynx is pulled up and forward, and the epiglottis tips over its opening
Breathing speeds up to keep oxygen flowing during the swallow
The pharyngeal constrictors squeeze the bolus down into the esophagus

q: A patient is given atropine, which blocks muscarinic receptor proteins. Predict the change in each variable in his mouth.

variables.name: Ability to taste a dry cracker

q: A 7-year-old who missed his vaccinations has a fever and painful swelling in front of and below both ears, so his cheeks look puffy. Which glands are swollen?
options: The submandibular glands
The sublingual glands
The parotid glands
The palatine tonsils

q: Salivary amylase is swallowed with a bolus of bread. What stops it from continuing to digest the starch?
options: It stops working at the back of the throat, where there is no more saliva
Stomach acid gradually soaks into the bolus and lowers its pH
The lower esophageal sphincter filters it out of the bolus
Bile from the gallbladder breaks it down

q: Select every component of saliva that protects the mouth and teeth from bacteria or acid.
options: Lysozyme
IgA antibodies
Bicarbonate
Salivary amylase
Mucus
Bile

q: A patient is given a drug that blocks transmission at the neuromuscular junctions of skeletal muscle but has no effect on smooth muscle. Which part of the esophagus loses its peristalsis?
options: The upper third
The lower third
The whole length equally
The middle third only

q: A 45-year-old man has a burning pain behind his sternum most nights when he lies down soon after a large dinner. It eases with antacids. What is the most likely cause?
options: Reduced blood flow to the heart muscle through narrowed coronary arteries
Stomach contents flowing back past the lower esophageal sphincter
A piece of food stuck at the upper esophageal sphincter
Inflammation and swelling of both parotid glands

q: Fill the gap: A swallow begins → vagal fibers activate enteric inhibitory neurons in the lower esophageal sphincter → ______ → the sphincter relaxes → the bolus enters the stomach
options: The neurons release nitric oxide onto the sphincter's smooth muscle
The neurons release acetylcholine onto skeletal muscle fibers of the sphincter
The neurons release norepinephrine onto alpha-1 receptor proteins on the muscle
Gravity pushes the sphincter open

q: Why does acid reflux damage the esophagus while the same acid does not damage the stomach that holds it all day?
options: The esophagus has a thicker muscle layer that the acid can reach more easily
Its stratified squamous lining lacks the stomach lining's acid defenses
The esophagus has a serosa that absorbs acid
Acid is stronger in the esophagus than in the stomach

q: A child's tongue cannot stick out past her lower teeth, and its tip forms a notch when she tries. Which structure is most likely too short?
options: The labial frenulum
The uvula
The lingual frenulum
The soft palate

q: A person has a hiatal hernia: the top of the stomach has slid up through the opening in the diaphragm, so the diaphragm no longer wraps the lower esophageal sphincter. Predict the change in each variable after a large meal.

variables.name: Pressure holding the lower esophageal sphincter closed
Episodes of reflux into the esophagus
Time for a bolus to travel down the esophagus

q: Name the pinned region of the stomach.
options: Fundus
Cardia
Body
Pyloric antrum

fig.alt: A J-shaped pouch cut open from the front. The esophagus enters at the top; a dome rises beside that entry on the right of the drawing, and the large middle region curves down and across to a narrowing tube on the left that ends at a thick muscular ring leading into the intestine. Three muscle layers are peeled back on the front wall, running lengthwise, around and diagonally. The inner lining is thrown into long folds. Arrows mark the short inner curve and the long outer curve.

q: Name the pinned cell of the gastric gland.
options: Chief cell
Parietal cell
Enteroendocrine cell
Mucous neck cell

fig.alt: Three panels of the stomach wall at increasing magnification. A small stomach shows where the sample comes from. A block of wall shows the lining dotted with pits that lead down into tube-shaped glands, then a thin muscle layer, a connective tissue layer with vessels, three layers of muscle running in different directions and a thin outer covering. An enlarged gland shows large round cells with folded interiors near its upper part, many smaller cells with granules lower down, and a few pale hormone-secreting cells at its base.

q: Name the pinned folds of the stomach lining.
options: Rugae
Gastric pits
Oblique layer
Lesser curvature

fig.alt: A J-shaped pouch cut open from the front. The esophagus enters at the top; a dome rises beside that entry on the right of the drawing, and the large middle region curves down and across to a narrowing tube on the left that ends at a thick muscular ring leading into the intestine. Three muscle layers are peeled back on the front wall, running lengthwise, around and diagonally. The inner lining is thrown into long folds. Arrows mark the short inner curve and the long outer curve.

q: Put the steps of acid secretion by a parietal cell in order.
options: Carbon dioxide and water combine inside the cell, sped up by carbonic anhydrase
Carbonic acid splits into H+ and bicarbonate
The H+/K+ ATPase spends ATP to pump H+ into the lumen in exchange for K+
Cl− leaves the cell into the lumen through channels
H+ and Cl− form hydrochloric acid in the lumen of the gland

q: A patient with a peptic ulcer takes a proton pump inhibitor, which blocks the H+/K+ ATPase of parietal cells. Predict the change in each variable after a meal, compared with before treatment.

variables.name: Bicarbonate added to the blood by the stomach (alkaline tide)

q: Which cell of the gastric glands secretes pepsinogen?
options: Parietal cell
Chief cell
G cell
Surface mucous cell

q: Fill the gap: Chief cells release pepsinogen into the gland → ______ → pepsin activates more pepsinogen → proteins are split into polypeptides
options: Bicarbonate in the mucus layer converts pepsinogen into pepsin
Intrinsic factor binds pepsinogen and switches on its active site
Gastrin reaches the gland lumen and cuts a piece off pepsinogen
Acid makes pepsinogen cut itself into pepsin

q: Why can chief cells store large amounts of pepsinogen without damaging themselves?
options: Chief cells contain no protein for the enzyme to digest
Pepsinogen is stored bound to intrinsic factor, which blocks its active site
Pepsinogen stays inactive until acid converts it
A layer of mucus surrounds each granule inside the chief cell

q: A 60-year-old woman has anemia with unusually large red blood cells. Tests show antibodies against her parietal cells. Her doctor prescribes vitamin B12 injections. Why not simply advise her to eat more foods rich in B12?
options: Her stomach acid destroys the B12 in her food before it can be absorbed
B12 in food is digested by pepsin into inactive fragments in her stomach
Her liver can no longer store B12, so she needs a steady supply by injection
She lacks intrinsic factor, so she cannot absorb B12 from food

q: A woman takes high-dose ibuprofen daily for arthritis and develops a stomach ulcer, though her acid secretion is normal. How does the drug make an ulcer more likely?
options: It blocks prostaglandin production, weakening the mucosal barrier
It raises gastrin release, so her stomach secretes much more acid than before
It kills the surface mucous cells directly on contact, as a detergent would
It activates pepsinogen while it is still stored inside the chief cells

q: Select every feature that helps protect the stomach lining from its own acid and pepsin.
options: A thick mucus layer with bicarbonate trapped in it
Tight junctions between the epithelial cells
Replacement of surface cells every few days
Prostaglandins made in the mucosa
Pepsin working best at neutral pH
Stratified squamous epithelium lining the stomach

q: This pathway describes control of acid secretion during the gastric phase. Which step is wrong?
options: Protein fragments in the stomach stimulate G cells
G cells release gastrin into the blood
Gastrin increases acid secretion, partly by releasing histamine
The stomach contents become strongly acidic
The falling pH makes the G cells release even more gastrin

q: In a physiology experiment, a volunteer chews a tasty meal and spits it out without swallowing (sham feeding). Predict the change in each variable, compared with before the meal.
Walking past a bakery, you smell fresh bread and your stomach begins to secrete acid. Which phase of gastric secretion is this?
options: Cephalic phase
Gastric phase
Intestinal phase
Esophageal phase

q: Two friends eat meals with the same calories. One eats plain rice and the other a fatty cheeseburger. An hour later, the cheeseburger eater's stomach is much fuller. What mainly explains the difference?
options: Fat stretches the stomach more, and stretch weakens its mixing waves
Fat raises gastrin release, and gastrin tightens the pyloric sphincter
Fat in the small intestine releases CCK and triggers the enterogastric reflex
Rice is absorbed through the stomach wall, so less of it remains to empty

q: During a mixing wave, the pyloric sphincter closes as the wave reaches it. What does this closure do to the stomach's contents?
options: It pushes all of the stomach's contents into the small intestine at once
It lets a little through and throws the rest back, grinding it
It stops all mixing until the stomach is stretched by the next meal
It sends the contents back up into the esophagus

q: A 3-year-old has vomited repeatedly for two days. Which change in her blood is most likely?
options: Acidosis, with low bicarbonate
A rise in blood potassium
No lasting change in blood pH
Alkalosis, with high bicarbonate

q: Which muscles supply the force that expels the stomach's contents during vomiting?
options: The stomach's three layers of smooth muscle, contracting from the pylorus upward
The esophageal muscle, pulling contents up by reverse peristalsis
The diaphragm and abdominal wall muscles squeezing the stomach
The pyloric sphincter, pushing the contents back toward the esophagus
misconception: the stomach forcefully contracts to vomit

q: An H2 blocker blocks only the histamine signal to parietal cells, yet it reduces acid secretion stimulated by food by well over half. Why is the effect so large?
options: Histamine is the only signal that parietal cells respond to
The drug also blocks the proton pump on the parietal cell membrane
Blocking histamine raises somatostatin release, which then blocks the pump
The three stimuli amplify each other, and gastrin acts largely via histamine

q: Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomach despite its acid. How does it survive?
options: It lives inside parietal cells, well away from the acid in the gland lumen
It forms tough spores that acid cannot damage
It stops the parietal cells around it from secreting any acid
It lives in the mucus and makes an enzyme whose product neutralizes acid

q: Name the pinned region of the small intestine.
options: Duodenum
Jejunum
Ileum
Large intestine

The pale, wider large intestine frames the coils, ending at the rectum below.

q: Name the pinned region of the small intestine.
options: Jejunum
Ileum
Duodenum
Pyloric antrum

fig.alt: A front view of the abdomen showing the small intestine in three colors. A short, curved first part sits at the top, where the stomach would empty into it. The middle part coils in the upper left of the abdomen, and the final part coils lower down on the right and in the pelvis. The pale, wider large intestine frames the coils, ending at the rectum below.

q: A surgeon removes a patient's last meter of small intestine because of disease. Which lifelong treatment is the patient most likely to need?
options: Tablets of lactase taken with every meal
Drugs that reduce stomach acid secretion
Injections of vitamin B12
Injections of insulin before meals

q: Which region of the small intestine has the most Peyer's patches?
options: Ileum
Duodenum
Jejunum
They are spread evenly along its length

q: Why does the first part of the duodenum contain glands that secrete a thick, alkaline mucus?
options: It is where most fat is absorbed into the lacteals of the villi
It is where the migrating motor complex begins between meals
It receives acidic chyme before pancreatic bicarbonate mixes in
It is where vitamin B12 is absorbed with intrinsic factor

q: Textbooks estimate that circular folds multiply the small intestine's surface about 3 times, villi about 10 times and microvilli about 20 times. A disease flattens the villi but leaves the folds and microvilli. By roughly how much does the absorptive surface fall?
options: To about half of normal
To about one tenth of normal
To about one twentieth of normal
It stays about the same

q: Put these structures of the small intestine in order of size, from largest to smallest.
options: Circular fold
Villus
Absorptive cell
Microvillus

q: Select every enzyme that is built into the brush border of the small intestine's absorptive cells.
options: Lactase
Sucrase
Pepsin
Maltase
Salivary amylase
Peptidases
misconception: intestinal juice is full of enzymes

q: Fill the gap: A child drinks milk → lactose reaches the small intestine → ______ → glucose and galactose are absorbed by the absorptive cells
options: Pepsin carried from the stomach splits lactose in the lumen
Intestinal juice from the glands splits lactose in the lumen
Lactose is absorbed whole and split later inside the liver
Brush border lactase splits it into glucose and galactose

q: A person who has not eaten since the evening before eats a large breakfast. Predict the change in each variable over the next half hour, compared with before the meal.

variables.name: Migrating motor complexes in the small intestine

q: After a fatty meal, the lymph in the lymphatic vessels of the mesentery looks milky white. Why?
options: Milk proteins are absorbed whole from the lumen into the lymph
White blood cells in the lymph multiply rapidly after every meal
Mucus from intestinal juice drains into the lymph vessels
Absorbed fat, in droplets too big for capillaries, enters lacteals

q: During a cholera outbreak, a man passes liters of watery stool a day. Cholera toxin locks open the chloride channels of the cells in his intestinal glands. Why does this produce so much water loss?
options: Chloride pours into the lumen and water follows, outpacing reabsorption
The toxin destroys the villi, so no water is absorbed at all
Chloride enters the gland cells and draws water out of the lumen
The toxin blocks the lacteals, so fluid backs up into the intestine

q: A patient receiving chemotherapy, which kills rapidly dividing cells, develops sores in the mouth and a damaged, leaky intestinal lining within a week. Why is the intestinal lining so quickly affected?
options: Chemotherapy is concentrated in bile, which is secreted into the intestine
Its stem cells divide constantly, renewing the lining every few days
The villi are made of smooth muscle, which chemotherapy targets directly
The drug digests the brush border enzymes on the microvilli

q: How do the circular folds of the small intestine differ from the rugae of the stomach?
options: Circular folds flatten when the intestine fills, but rugae do not
Circular folds are folds of muscle, while rugae are folds of serosa
Circular folds are microscopic, while rugae can be seen by eye
Circular folds are permanent ridges; rugae flatten as the stomach fills

q: In a fasting person, a band of strong peristaltic contraction starts in the stomach about every 90 to 120 minutes and travels down to the ileum. What is this pattern for, and what triggers it?
options: It mixes chyme with pancreatic secretions, triggered by secretin
It clears residue and bacteria, triggered by motilin
It empties bile from the gallbladder, triggered by CCK after a meal
It relaxes the ileocecal sphincter after meals, triggered by gastrin

q: Priya has celiac disease, and her villi are flattened. She gets bloating and loose stools after milk but not after plain rice. Which brush border change best explains this?
options: Her pancreas has stopped secreting its digestive enzymes into the duodenum
Her stomach no longer secretes pepsin because of the immune reaction
She has lost most lactase, the scarcest brush border enzyme
She has lost her maltase, so she cannot digest the starch in rice

q: This pathway follows starch through the small intestine. Which step is wrong?
options: Enzymes from the pancreas split starch in the lumen into maltose and short chains
Segmentation presses the maltose against the brush border
Maltase in the microvillus membrane splits maltose into two glucose
Glucose enters the lacteal in the core of the villus
The blood carries glucose from the intestine to the liver

q: A surgeon opening the abdomen finds a loop of small intestine with a thick, red wall and tall, closely packed circular folds inside. Which region is this most likely to be?
options: Jejunum
Ileum
Duodenum
The first part of the large intestine

q: Name the pinned structures.
options: Bile canaliculi
Sinusoids
Central veins
Portal venules

Hepatic vein
Bile duct

options: Common hepatic duct
Common bile duct
Right hepatic duct
Cystic duct

q: Name the pinned duct.
options: Common bile duct
Pancreatic duct
Cystic duct
Left hepatic duct

q: Trace bile made by a hepatocyte, stored in the gallbladder and released after a meal. Put the steps in order.
options: A hepatocyte secretes bile into a bile canaliculus, which carries it to a bile duct in a portal triad
Bile drains through a hepatic duct into the common hepatic duct
Bile flows up the cystic duct into the gallbladder, which concentrates it
After a meal, the gallbladder contracts and bile flows down the cystic duct
Bile flows down the common bile duct to the hepatopancreatic ampulla
Bile enters the duodenum at the major duodenal papilla

q: A drug is swallowed and absorbed from the small intestine. Before it reaches the heart, where does it first meet hepatocytes?
options: In the sinusoids of liver lobules, after arriving in the hepatic portal vein
In the central veins of the lobules, after arriving through the hepatic artery from the aorta
In the bile canaliculi, after arriving in the common bile duct
In the hepatic veins, after passing through the inferior vena cava

variables.name: pH of the chyme in the duodenum

q: Complete the sequence: trypsinogen reaches the duodenum → ____ on the brush border cuts it → active trypsin forms → trypsin activates chymotrypsinogen and more trypsinogen.
options: Enteropeptidase
Pepsin
Cholecystokinin
Pancreatic amylase

q: Bile contains no enzymes. How, then, does it speed up the digestion of fat?
options: Its bicarbonate splits the bonds that hold fatty acids to glycerol
Its bilirubin activates pancreatic lipase
Its bile salts break fat into many small droplets
Its cholesterol dissolves the fat into the water

q: Fat droplets 0.5 mm across are emulsified into droplets 0.005 mm across, keeping the same total volume. By what factor does the fat's total surface area change?
options: It rises 10-fold
It rises 100-fold
It rises 10,000-fold
It does not change

q: A 34-year-old woman had the last part of her ileum removed because of Crohn disease. Months later she has pale, greasy stools after fatty meals. Her liver, gallbladder and pancreas are normal. What best explains her symptoms?
options: Her gallbladder can no longer concentrate bile
Her pancreas no longer releases lipase in response to fat
Her bile salts are lost instead of being recycled
Her liver has stopped conjugating bilirubin

q: A student described what happens when a fatty meal reaches the duodenum. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Fat in the chyme makes duodenal enteroendocrine cells release cholecystokinin
Cholecystokinin travels in the blood to the gallbladder and the pancreas
Cholecystokinin makes the gallbladder's smooth muscle contract
Cholecystokinin contracts the hepatopancreatic sphincter
Bile and enzyme-rich pancreatic juice flow into the duodenum

q: An experiment infuses acid into a volunteer's duodenum. Which change in pancreatic secretion follows?
options: A small volume of juice rich in enzymes, driven by cholecystokinin
A large volume of juice rich in bicarbonate, driven by secretin
No change in pancreatic secretion
Juice rich in trypsin, activated inside the pancreatic duct

q: A 52-year-old man with gallstones has sudden, severe pain in his upper middle abdomen that goes through to his back. His blood lipase is many times normal. Which event most likely started his illness?
options: Bile salts leaked from the liver into the blood and dissolved the pancreas
A stone blocked the cystic duct and stopped bile from reaching the duodenum after his meals
Stomach acid flowed back up the pancreatic duct and burned the pancreas
A stone at the ampulla blocked the pancreatic duct, so trypsin was activated in the gland

q: Select every job that hepatocytes do.
options: Make albumin
Make clotting factors
Store glycogen
Make insulin
Make bile salts from cholesterol
Make pancreatic lipase

q: A 60-year-old man with cirrhosis has a swollen, fluid-filled abdomen and swollen ankles. His blood albumin is low. Which two changes together best explain the fluid?
options: Raised pressure in the hepatic portal vein, and less albumin holding water in the blood
Blocked bile ducts, and too much bilirubin in the blood pulling water out of the vessels
Loss of bile salts, and poor fat absorption thinning the blood
Too many clotting factors, and blood clots blocking the veins

q: Blood and bile both move through a liver lobule. How do their directions compare?
options: Both flow outward from the central vein to the portal triads
Both flow inward from the portal triads to the central vein
Blood flows inward to the central vein; bile flows outward to the portal triads
Blood flows outward to the portal triads; bile flows inward and drains into the central vein

q: Between meals, the liver keeps making bile. What makes that bile end up in the gallbladder rather than the duodenum?
options: The gallbladder pumps bile up the common bile duct
The hepatopancreatic sphincter is closed and bile backs up the cystic duct
Secretin closes the common hepatic duct
Cholecystokinin relaxes the gallbladder wall and draws bile in

q: A person takes a large overdose of acetaminophen. Why is the liver the organ most damaged?
options: The liver stores the drug in hepatocytes instead of excreting it in bile or urine
Acetaminophen blocks the hepatic artery
Liver enzymes turn some of the drug into a reactive product that kills hepatocytes
Acetaminophen dissolves the bile salts inside the canaliculi and blocks bile flow

q: Name the pinned cells.
options: Pancreatic islet cells
Acinar cells
Duct cells
Hepatocytes

fig.alt: Top: the pancreas, a long pale lobulated organ, with its broad head tucked into the curve of the first part of the small intestine and its narrow tail extending to the right; a main duct runs its length and joins the bile duct. Bottom: an enlarged square of pancreatic tissue. Most of it is round clusters of pink cells around tiny ducts that drain into a larger green duct, labeled as exocrine cells secreting pancreatic juice and acinar cells secreting digestive enzymes. Two pale blue-green islands of cells with capillaries running through them are labeled as pancreatic islet cells secreting hormones.

q: Why does the pancreas release its protein-digesting enzymes as trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen rather than as active trypsin and chymotrypsin?
options: Active enzymes inside the gland would digest the acinar cells and ducts
The active forms are too large to pass through the pancreatic duct
The precursors digest protein faster in the acid of the stomach
The active forms would be destroyed by bile salts

q: Name the pinned region.
options: Ileum
Sigmoid colon
Cecum
Ascending colon

From there a gray-green, puckered tube rises up the right side, bends sharply under where the liver would be, crosses the abdomen, bends down again higher on the left, descends the left side and makes an S-shaped loop in the pelvis. It joins a purple straight segment that ends in a short canal at the bottom.

q: Name the pinned region.
options: Descending colon
Sigmoid colon
Rectum
Transverse colon

fig.alt: A front view of the large intestine framing the faded coils of the small intestine. A yellow-green pouch in the lower right receives the end of the small intestine, with a small worm-like tube hanging below it. From there a gray-green, puckered tube rises up the right side, bends sharply under where the liver would be, crosses the abdomen, bends down again higher on the left, descends the left side and makes an S-shaped loop in the pelvis. It joins a purple straight segment that ends in a short canal at the bottom.

q: Name the pinned structure.
options: Epiploic appendages
Haustra
Mesentery
Teniae coli

fig.alt: A close view of the outer surface of the colon. The wall bulges into a row of rounded pouches. A narrow pale yellow ribbon of muscle runs lengthwise down the tube, and small yellow fat-filled tags hang from the surface along it.

q: Name the pinned structures.
options: Haustra
Circular folds
Villi
Rugae

fig.alt: A close view of the outer surface of the colon. The wall bulges into a row of rounded pouches. A narrow pale yellow ribbon of muscle runs lengthwise down the tube, and small yellow fat-filled tags hang from the surface along it.

q: Put the steps of the defecation reflex in order, starting from a mass movement.
options: A mass movement pushes feces into the rectum
The rectal wall stretches and its stretch-sensitive sensory receptors fire
Sensory neurons carry the signal to the sacral spinal cord
Parasympathetic neurons make the rectum contract and the internal anal sphincter relax
You choose to relax the external anal sphincter
Feces pass out through the anal canal

q: About 9 L of fluid enter your gut each day from food, drink and secretions. Where is most of it absorbed?
options: In the stomach, before chyme leaves it
In the colon, where feces take shape
In the small intestine
In the rectum
misconception: the colon absorbs most of the water

q: How does the colon absorb water?
options: Carrier proteins pump water molecules across the epithelium using ATP
It actively absorbs sodium, and water follows by osmosis
Bacteria in the lumen take up water and carry it into the wall
Contractions of the haustra force water through the lining

q: A patient starts taking an opioid pain drug, which slows the movements of the colon. Predict the change in each variable over the following days.

variables.name: Time feces spend in the colon
Water absorbed from each day's contents

q: A 74-year-old woman finishes a two-week course of a broad-spectrum antibiotic for pneumonia. A week later she has frequent watery diarrhea, cramps and fever. Stool tests find toxins from Clostridioides difficile. Which explanation fits best?
options: The antibiotic thinned her normal colon bacteria, and a resistant species overgrew and made toxins
The antibiotic damaged her teniae coli and sped up her colon
The antibiotic blocked her colon's sodium channels and stopped water absorption
The antibiotic made her pancreas stop secreting enzymes

q: Select every job done by the bacteria of the colon.
options: Fermenting fiber into short-chain fatty acids and gas
Turning bilirubin into stercobilin
Making some vitamins, including vitamin K
Secreting bile salts
Crowding out harmful microbes
Absorbing most of the water in the colon

q: What forms the haustra of the colon?
options: Fat-filled pouches of peritoneum that hang from the outer surface of the colon
Circular folds of the mucosa that trap chyme
Villi arranged in rings
Longitudinal muscle gathered into three bands shorter than the wall

q: A 30-year-old man has a spinal cord injury at T6. His sacral cord is intact. After a mass movement fills his rectum, what happens?
options: Nothing happens until signals arrive from the brain
The rectum contracts by reflex, but he feels no urge and has no voluntary control
He feels the urge normally, but his rectum cannot contract to push the feces out
His internal sphincter stays closed, but he can relax his external sphincter at will

q: A student described the anal sphincters. One statement is wrong. Which one?
options: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle
The internal anal sphincter relaxes by reflex when the rectum stretches
The external anal sphincter is smooth muscle controlled by the enteric nervous system
The external anal sphincter lets you delay defecation
A Valsalva's maneuver raises pressure inside the abdomen

q: A traveler with cholera passes more than 10 L of watery stool a day. The toxin makes his intestinal lining secrete chloride into the lumen. Why does the colon fail to prevent the diarrhea?
options: The toxin destroys the colon's lining cells, so the colon can no longer absorb water
The colon stops moving and fluid pools in it and leaks out
Chloride blocks the colon's sodium channels
The fluid arriving far exceeds the colon's maximum absorption of about 4 to 5 L a day

q: A child eats a large bag of sugar-free candy sweetened with sorbitol, which the gut absorbs poorly. By what mechanism does diarrhea follow?
options: Secretory: sorbitol makes the lining secrete chloride
Osmotic: unabsorbed sorbitol holds water in the lumen
Inflammatory: sorbitol damages the epithelial cells
Reflex: sorbitol triggers the defecation reflex directly

q: Many people feel the urge to defecate soon after breakfast. What explains this?
options: The gastrocolic reflex: stomach stretch triggers mass movements in the colon
Breakfast is digested so fast that its remains reach the rectum within minutes
Coffee and food relax the external anal sphincter
Morning cortisol from the adrenal cortex contracts the teniae coli

q: Which comparison between the small and large intestine is correct?
options: The large intestine is longer as well as wider than the small intestine
The large intestine has villi and the small intestine does not
The small intestine has teniae coli and the large intestine does not
The large intestine has more goblet cells and no villi

q: Complete the route of contents through the large intestine: cecum → ascending colon → transverse colon → descending colon → ____ → rectum → anal canal.
options: Sigmoid colon
Ileum
Appendix
Right colic flexure

q: A child has had severe watery diarrhea for two days. Predict the change in each variable in the child's blood and body, compared with before the illness.
Why does a high-fiber diet usually relieve constipation?
options: Fiber is digested into glucose, which speeds colon movements
Fiber holds water in the stool and adds bulk that stretches the colon wall
Fiber blocks the sodium pumps of the colon's epithelial cells and stops water absorption
Fiber kills the gut bacteria that slow transit

q: Why do gut bacteria thrive in the colon but stay sparse in the stomach and upper small intestine?
options: The colon secretes sugars and amino acids into its lumen that feed the bacteria living there
The colon has no mucus layer to keep bacteria away from its lining cells
Upstream, acid and fast flow keep them down; the colon is slow, oxygen-poor and fiber-rich
Bile salts are made in the colon and feed bacteria there

q: Name the pinned vessel.
options: Blood capillary
Lacteal
Hepatic portal vein
Central vein

fig.alt: A cross-section of the intestinal lining. At the top, in the lumen, large round fat droplets become small spiky droplets (an emulsion) and then tiny clusters (micelles). From a micelle, a small lipid droplet crosses the brush border of an absorptive cell. Inside the cell it joins others near the green Golgi apparatus, is packed into a small round particle, and leaves through the bottom of the cell. Below the cell, the particle enters a pale green blind-ended lymph vessel (a lacteal) that sits inside a loop of red blood capillary.

q: Name the pinned enzyme.
options: Sucrase
Maltase
Lactase
α-Dextrinase

fig.alt: A flow chart. A top box of starch and glycogen is cut by salivary amylase into two groups: short branched polysaccharides (limit dextrins) on the left and three disaccharides on the right, maltose, sucrose and lactose. Below each, an enzyme is named: alpha-dextrinase, maltase, sucrase and lactase. The bottom boxes give the monosaccharides produced: glucose from the dextrins; two glucose from maltose; one glucose and one fructose from sucrose; one glucose and one galactose from lactose.

q: Put the steps of starch digestion and absorption in order.
options: Salivary amylase starts cutting starch in the mouth
Pancreatic amylase cuts starch into maltose, maltotriose and α-dextrins in the small intestine
Brush border maltase and α-dextrinase split these into glucose
Glucose enters the absorptive cell with sodium through SGLT1
Glucose leaves the cell by facilitated diffusion across the basolateral membrane
Glucose travels in the hepatic portal vein to the liver

q: Put the steps of protein digestion and absorption in order.
options: Pepsin cuts proteins into large polypeptides in the stomach
Trypsin and chymotrypsin cut the polypeptides into shorter peptides in the duodenum
Carboxypeptidase and brush border aminopeptidase remove amino acids from the chain ends
Amino acids, dipeptides and tripeptides enter the absorptive cells on carriers
Peptidases inside the cell split dipeptides and tripeptides into amino acids
Amino acids leave the cell and enter the villus capillaries

q: Put the steps of fat digestion and absorption in order.
options: Bile salts emulsify fat into tiny droplets
Pancreatic lipase splits triglycerides into fatty acids and monoglycerides
Micelles carry fatty acids and monoglycerides to the brush border
Fatty acids and monoglycerides enter the absorptive cell and are rebuilt into triglycerides
Triglycerides are packaged into chylomicrons and leave the cell by exocytosis
Chylomicrons enter a lacteal and travel in lymph to the thoracic duct

q: An adult with low lactase drinks two large glasses of milk on an empty stomach. Predict the change in each variable over the next few hours, compared with a person with high lactase drinking the same milk.

variables.name: Water in the lumen of the small intestine
Rise in blood glucose after drinking

q: A patient takes a weight-loss drug that blocks pancreatic lipase in the gut. Predict the change in each variable after a fatty meal, compared with the same meal without the drug.

variables.name: Absorption of vitamin D from the meal
Glucose absorption from the meal's starch

q: In an experiment on intestinal tissue, a drug blocks the sodium–potassium pumps on the basolateral membrane of the absorptive cells. SGLT1 itself is untouched. What happens to glucose absorption?
options: It stops once sodium inside the cell rises and the gradient collapses
It continues unchanged
It speeds up
It continues at the same rate by facilitated diffusion

q: A child with cholera is losing liters of watery stool. The toxin makes the intestinal lining secrete chloride, and sodium and water follow. Nurses give a drink of water, salt and glucose. Why does the glucose help?
options: Glucose kills the cholera bacteria in the lumen
Glucose blocks the chloride secretion caused by the toxin
Glucose pulls sodium in through SGLT1, and water follows
Glucose is the main fuel the child's colon needs to absorb water

q: Using the figure, what share of the fluid that reaches the colon does the colon absorb?
options: About 14%
About 89%
About 50%
Nearly 98%

q: Why do absorbed long-chain fats reach the blood through the lymph instead of entering the villus capillaries directly?
options: Bile salts carry the fats straight into the lacteals
Lymph moves faster than blood through the villus
The villus capillaries are continuous, with an unbroken wall
Chylomicrons are too large for the blood capillaries

options: Long-chain fatty acids
Vitamin K
Glucose
Cholesterol
Amino acids
Vitamin D

q: A 45-year-old man had the last meter of his ileum removed eight years ago. He eats a normal diet and his stomach is healthy. He now has a large-cell anemia and numb feet. What is the most likely cause?
options: Loss of the site where B12 bound to intrinsic factor is absorbed
Loss of intrinsic factor production
Loss of pancreatic proteases that free B12 from haptocorrin
Loss of the lactase needed to absorb B12

q: Complete the route of vitamin B12: acid and pepsin free B12 from food and it binds haptocorrin → ____ → B12 binds intrinsic factor → the complex is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
options: Pancreatic proteases digest haptocorrin in the duodenum
Bile salts carry B12 into micelles in the jejunum
Lactase splits B12 away from haptocorrin at the brush border
Chylomicrons carry B12 into the lacteals of the villi

q: A 25-year-old woman gets bloating, gas and loose stools about two hours after drinking milk, but eats hard cheese without trouble. She has never had hives or wheezing. Which explanation fits best?
options: A milk allergy: IgE against milk proteins
Low lactase: lactose reaches her colon and is fermented
A pancreatic lipase deficiency: she cannot digest milk fat
Too much lactase: glucose floods her colon

q: A student described what happens to fat after lipase has digested it. One step is wrong. Which one?
options: Fatty acids and monoglycerides join bile salts in micelles
At the brush border they leave the micelles and enter the absorptive cell
The smooth endoplasmic reticulum rebuilds them into triglycerides
Triglycerides are packaged with cholesterol and protein into chylomicrons
Chylomicrons enter the villus blood capillaries and go to the liver in the hepatic portal vein

q: What are the final products of nucleic acid digestion that the absorptive cells take up?
options: Whole nucleotides, taken up intact by carriers
Amino acids and glucose from the nucleic acid chains
Short RNA chains, taken up by endocytosis
Pentose sugars, nitrogenous bases and phosphate

q: A child has an inherited defect in the brush border carrier for a group of neutral amino acids. Yet blood levels of those amino acids after a protein meal are only mildly low. What best explains this?
options: Those amino acids diffuse freely through the lipid bilayer of the brush border
Much of them enters inside dipeptides and tripeptides on another carrier
The colon absorbs all the amino acids the small intestine misses
Pepsin converts them into other amino acids that use working carriers

q: Celiac disease flattens the villi and damages the brush border. After a starchy meal, which products would you expect to build up in the lumen?
options: Whole starch
Glucose
Maltose and α-dextrins
Galactose

q: Which statement about carboxypeptidase is correct?
options: It comes from the pancreas and removes amino acids from the carboxyl end of a chain
It is fixed to the brush border and removes amino acids from the amino end of a chain
It is made by the stomach's chief cells and works best in acid
It digests carbohydrates that carry carboxyl groups

q: A 70-year-old man has had a tumor blocking his common bile duct for two months. He is jaundiced and now bleeds for a long time from a small cut. His liver cells are still healthy. What links the blocked duct to the bleeding?
options: Bilirubin in the blood destroys the circulating platelets
Without bile salts, vitamin K is poorly absorbed
The tumor releases heparin-like molecules into the blood
Blocked bile makes the liver stop making fibrinogen and albumin

q: Fructose enters absorptive cells by facilitated diffusion rather than with sodium. What follows from this for fructose absorption?
options: It needs the lumen to hold more fructose than the cell
Fructose absorption uses more ATP than glucose absorption
Fructose is absorbed into lacteals instead of capillaries
Fructose absorption stops when sodium is absent from the lumen

q: Some fatty acids in milk have short chains. How does their route into the body differ from that of long-chain fatty acids?
options: They cannot be absorbed at all
They are absorbed in the colon, packaged into chylomicrons
They cross the cell unchanged and enter the blood capillaries
They are absorbed in the terminal ileum with intrinsic factor
